opus-5.5.text:
That's a big question. Let me answer it through a few people whose work shaped how I think.

The first is probably Kaiming He. I was lucky to work closely with him at FAIR, and ResNet is the obvious example. What strikes me about that paper isn't complexity, it's the opposite. The core idea is almost embarrassingly simple: add an identity shortcut and let the network learn a residual. But it came from really understanding a problem, the degradation problem, where deeper networks weren't even fitting the training data well. He didn't paper over that with tricks. He asked why it happens and found the minimal change that fixes it. From that I learned that good research is often about subtraction, finding the one thing that matters and stripping away everything else. And a truly good idea becomes infrastructure. People stop citing it consciously because it's just how things are built.

Then there's my PhD advisor, Zhuowen Tu. Our work on holistically-nested edge detection and on deeply-supervised nets taught me something different: taste in problems. He always pushed me to ask whether a problem is fundamental or just fashionable. A lot of papers solve a benchmark. Fewer change how you think about representation or learning.

And Yann LeCun, of course. Whether or not you agree with all of his views, his career shows what conviction looks like. He believed in convolutional networks and learned representations through decades when the field wasn't paying attention. That taught me research isn't only about being clever in the moment. It's about having a long-term belief about what intelligence requires and being willing to be unpopular for a while.

So if I put those together, I think research means a few things. It means honestly understanding a phenomenon rather than just chasing numbers. It means simplicity, because the ideas that last are usually ones you can explain on a whiteboard in five minutes. And it means having a worldview. Right now, for me, that's the belief that visual intelligence, understanding the physical world and not just language, is still deeply unsolved and central to building real intelligence.

The last thing I'd say is that the papers that influenced me most weren't necessarily the ones with the highest numbers. They were the ones that made me feel, after reading them, that the world was a bit clearer than before. That's what I hope my own work can do, even if only occasionally.

r001.rationale: The response draws lessons about research from influential researchers’ papers and says research means understanding phenomena and developing lasting ideas.

r002.rationale: The response does not reject publishing papers as the purpose of research.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I keep coming back to, and my answer has shifted a lot over the years.

When I was a student, I thought research meant writing papers. You find a problem, you beat the baseline, you get accepted. That's what it looked like from the outside. But the papers that actually changed how I think were never the ones with the best numbers in the table.

Kaiming He's ResNet paper is the obvious example, and I say that as someone who later worked with him on ResNeXt. What struck me about it wasn't the result. It was the restraint. The whole idea fits on one page. There's no exotic machinery, just a very honest observation: deeper networks were getting worse, and that shouldn't happen if the extra layers could simply learn identity. The paper takes that one contradiction seriously and refuses to let go of it. That taught me that research is often about noticing something slightly wrong that everyone else has already stepped over.

Then there's Yann LeCun, going back to the original convolutional network work. What I take from Yann is patience with an idea. He believed in a certain picture of how learning should work for decades, through periods when almost nobody cared. Research there isn't a sequence of papers, it's a long bet. The individual papers are just checkpoints along the way.

And Ross Girshick's R-CNN line of work taught me a third thing, which is that engineering is not beneath research. There's a kind of snobbery in academia where people want the clean theorem and look down on the messy system. Ross's papers are messy in the best sense. They are careful about details that matter in practice, and that care is itself a form of intellectual seriousness.

So if I put those together, I'd say the meaning of research, at least the way I've come to understand it, is something like this: find a tension that's real, hold onto it longer than is comfortable, and then be honest enough that the solution is as simple as it can be. The paper is just the artifact. The actual work is the way of looking.

What's interesting is that each of these people would probably describe it differently. And I think that's part of it too. You don't inherit a philosophy of research from your heroes. You borrow pieces, and eventually the mix becomes your own.

r001.rationale: The response draws lessons about research from ResNet, LeCun’s convolutional network work, and R-CNN papers, then combines those lessons into its understanding of research.

r002.rationale: It says the paper is only the artifact and describes the actual work as a way of looking, rejecting publication itself as research’s purpose.

astra-6.text:
For me, reading the papers of people who have influenced me is less about collecting their conclusions and more about understanding how they think. Why did they choose this problem? What did they notice that other people overlooked? And how did they turn an intuition into something they could test?

When you first start doing research, it’s easy to read a paper as a finished product. Everything seems logical, almost inevitable. But then you do research yourself, and you realize that the clean story probably came out of a very messy process. So I try to read backward: what was the uncertainty before this work existed? What was the decision that made the difference?

That has shaped what research means to me. It’s about developing judgment—knowing which questions are worth asking, which assumptions deserve to be challenged, and what evidence would actually change your mind. A result can be useful today and become obsolete later. But a way of asking questions can stay with you for a very long time. That’s the influence I value most.

r001.rationale: The response says that reading influential researchers’ papers helps reveal how they think, and frames research as developing judgment through that understanding.

r002.rationale: The response does not address publishing papers as the purpose of research or reject that idea.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, reading papers is a way of learning how someone thinks. The result matters, of course, but I’m more interested in why they chose that problem, which assumptions they questioned, and how they found a simple way to express the idea.

When someone’s work really influences you, it changes the questions you ask. You might initially admire a particular method, but later you realize that what stayed with you was their taste: their sense of what matters and what is worth pursuing.

That’s how I understand research. It’s a process of developing your own judgment. You learn from other people’s work, try things yourself, and gradually find questions you genuinely want to understand. A paper is one expression of that process; the deeper influence is how it changes your way of thinking.

r001.rationale: The response says reading papers helps you learn how influential researchers think, and frames research as learning from their work and developing your own judgment.

r002.rationale: It describes a paper as one expression of the research process and says the deeper influence is a change in how you think, so publishing papers is not presented as research’s purpose.
